title: Faith as trust
hook: the Greek word pistis means trust, faithfulness, loyalty

segments.voice: Yesterday, calling: a boy who heard his name at night and kept running to the wrong person. Your line was called to love. What one line did you write? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

"Master, master, we perish." A small boat filling with water, a storm of wind come down on the lake, and men shouting over the wind. Jesus is asleep in the boat. They wake him. He gets up, rebukes the wind and the waves, and there is a calm. Then he turns to his friends and asks one short question: "Where is your faith?" He doesn't ask what they believe about him. They'd just called him master. He asks where their faith went when the water came in. Today's word: faith as trust.

The New Testament's word for faith is pistis. In Greek it is a wide word. It can mean trust, it can mean faithfulness, and it can mean loyalty, the kind you keep to a friend. So when the Gospels talk about faith, they don't only mean holding a list of ideas to be true. They mean leaning your weight on someone. That's why the question in the boat lands so hard. The disciples ran to him for help. What they couldn't do, with the boat filling, was trust him. Luke even says that afterward they asked one another what manner of man this was. They were still working out who he was. The Letter to the Hebrews gives a picture of faith that is nearly all trust. Abraham is called, and "he went out, not knowing whither he went." No map. Just a voice, and his feet. The Proverbs put it plainly: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding." Lean. Faith as a weight you put down on someone. Churches describe faith in different ways. Martin Luther stressed faith as trust in God's promise. Catholic teaching speaks of faith as a personal clinging to God, and also as the mind's assent to what God has revealed. Orthodox writers describe it as a living relationship. They hold the parts together differently, but each of them has trust in it somewhere. And trust can live beside doubt. In Mark's Gospel a father with a sick son says to Jesus, in one breath: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both halves are spoken. And Jesus heals his son. Trust doesn't mean the storm is gone. It means you're still in the boat, with your weight on someone.

Here's the practice: trust someone. Settle, and breathe. Notice where you're holding your own weight right now: your shoulders, your jaw, your hands. Let the chair or the floor take it. That's a small trust already. Then think of one person you could lean on a little more today. Someone you could ask for help, or tell something true to, or hand a job you've been gripping. Picture doing it. If you pray, you can rest on the proverb's line: trust in the LORD with all thine heart. If you don't, just let the floor hold you. The bell holds the time.
Faith as trust. Pistis: not only believing something is true, but leaning your weight on someone, even in a storm, even with doubt beside it.

Your line: faith is trust. Today, do the thing you pictured: ask for the help, tell the truth, or hand over the job. Let someone take a little of your weight. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Christians speak of faith as trusting God in daily life, and some bring their worries to God in prayer, alone or by asking others in their church to pray with them.

original.note: Greek: faith, trust, faithfulness, loyalty — the New Testament's word for faith.

what it means: in the Gospels, faith is also trust, leaning your weight on someone, like friends in a boat in a storm.
what a scholar hears: pistis covers trust, faithfulness and loyalty. churches weigh trust and assent differently, but each keeps trust in it.

notes: The range of pistis (trust, faithfulness, loyalty) comes from the index hook; standard lexicons give faith/trust, faithfulness, and pledge/proof. Confirm 'loyalty'.

Church summaries: Luther (faith as trust, fiducia, in God's promise); Catholic teaching (CCC 150: personal adherence to God and assent to revealed truth; CCC 176); Orthodox 'living relationship'. Confirm each is fair and unranked.
